US WEEKLY KICKSTART
Corporate equity demand should outweigh record IPO supply in 2026

- IPO activity is continuing to recover after four years of muted issuance. 40 deals worth $28 billion have launched YTD, the largest totals through May since 2021. While elevated IPO activity has characterized some previous equity market peaks, the number of IPOs YTD is only on pace to reach the historical annual average of 100. In contrast, more than 250 IPOs launched in 2021 and nearly 400 launched in 1999.

2026 should be a record year for IPOs in dollar terms. Our IPO Barometer continues to signal a healthy macro backdrop for new launches, and news reports and prediction markets indicate an increased likelihood that some of the largest private companies will come public this year. We raise our forecast for 2026 IPO volume to $225 billion (from $160 billion). We expect total corporate equity supply to register $675 billion including follow-ons and other issuance. However, this issuance scales to just 1.0% of US equity market cap, compared to an average of 1.5% since 1995.

As investor lockups expire, IPO issuance leads to additional potential equity supply. History shows that large IPOs with initial floats of less than 10% experience an average increase in float to 46% 12 months later. Following this historical pattern, we expect nearly $500 billion in potential equity supply from expiring lockups in 2026. However, this post-lockup potential supply may not materialize if investors choose to maintain their ownership positions.

Buyback growth has slowed alongside the AI capex boom, rising just 4% y/y in Q1 2026. Because market values have continued to rise, the S&P 500 buyback yield has declined to 1.9%, near the lowest level since 2021. However, the magnitude of repurchases remains large and continues to grow. Financials account for 27% of S&P 500 buybacks and grew repurchases by 18% in Q1. NVDA announced an $80 billion authorization, and total buyback announcements are running at a record $860 billion YTD. We forecast gross corporate buybacks of $1.3 trillion this year.

Despite slow recent buyback growth and prospects for a record year for IPOs, corporate demand for equities should outweigh both direct corporate equity issuance and potential post-lockup equity supply in 2026. Strong M&A activity should bolster that balance; announcements have totaled nearly $900 billion YTD, 48% higher than this time last year, with nearly 70% cash consideration.

The balance of corporate equity supply and demand will become more challenging in 2027. The magnitude of post-lockup supply will depend on many factors, including the performance of IPOs, the size of initial floats, and investor desire for liquidity. However, post-lockup equity supply will likely increase in 2027 relative to 2026.

■ Outside of corporates, foreign investors represent a likely additional source of equity demand in coming months, as do households, who were net sellers in the late 1990s but have recently been buying US equities. In addition, much of the liquidity created by IPOs should eventually end up reinvested in the equity market. Changes in index inclusion rules should accelerate passive demand for some new issues.

The outlook for IPOs and the corporate equity supply/demand balance

US IPO activity has recently accelerated following four consecutive years of muted issuance. 24 US companies have come to market so far in Q2 2026, bringing the YTD total to 40. This represents more than double the number of IPOs at this point in 2025 and the largest total through May since the 95 IPOs launched in the first five months of 2021. Nonetheless, despite the recent pickup in activity, the number of deals so far this year has lagged the average total of 50 IPOs through May since 1995.
Exhibit 1: 40 US companies have gone public so far this year US deals greater than $25 million in value
Source: FactSet, GS Global Investment Research

US IPOs have raised $28 billion in gross proceeds YTD, the largest total at this point in the year since 2021. $44 billion was raised in the first five months of 2021. First day returns of recent IPOs indicate a healthy appetite for new issuance, with the average IPO in Q2 rising by 21% on its first trading day, in line with the historical average.

We estimate IPO gross proceeds will total a record $225 billion in 2026. Our previous forecast was for $160 billion of IPO issuance. Our new estimates reflect a continued healthy macro backdrop for IPOs, as signaled by our IPO Barometer (Exhibit 35), and recent changes to the outlook for potential launches by some of the largest private companies. Including follow-ons, converts, and SPACs, we estimate corporate equity issuance will total $675 billion this year.
Although we expect a record year in 2026 for corporate equity issuance, supply relative to the size of the equity market should remain below the long-term
average. Our estimate for $675 billion of corporate equity supply equates to 1% of Russell 3000 market cap, in line with average annual equity issuance from 2015-2019.

Based on the historical pattern, we estimate that recent and upcoming IPOs will result in roughly $500 billion of additional unlocked shares available to sell in 2026 and likely a larger quantity in 2027. We expect the majority of potential equity supply from the current pipeline of IPOs will become free float in 2027. Importantly, however, these shares will not necessarily translate to additional equity supply if investors choose to maintain their ownership in recent IPOs rather than sell those positions.

On the demand side of the equation, corporate buybacks have continued to give way to surging capex spending. S&P 500 buybacks rose by 4% year/year in Q1, continuing the recent trend of mid-single digit growth. We forecast S&P 500 buybacks will grow by 3% this year as capex growth exceeds 30%.

Source: FactSet, GS Global Investment Research

Despite weak recent buyback growth, US companies remain a large source of equity demand. We expect US companies will execute more than $1.3 trillion in buybacks in 2026. While hyperscaler buybacks fell by 64% year/year in Q1, growing buybacks from Banks and the beneficiaries of AI capex, such as semiconductors, should help offset some of those headwinds. NVDA, for example, added $80 billion to its buyback authorization following its latest report. In total, US companies have announced a record $860 billion in buyback authorizations YTD, 18% growth relative to this time last year.

M&A will be another source of corporate demand for US equity in coming quarters.

US M&A activity has been resilient this year despite market volatility, with almost $900 billion of announced transactions YTD (+48% year/year). Cash has represented roughly 70% of consideration for announced M&A this year, close to recent averages.

In addition to corporates, US households and foreign investors represent additional potential sources of US equity demand in coming months. While households were a significant source equity supply during the late 1990s, the group has recently been a net buyer of equities. The share of the corporate US equity market owned by foreign investors has risen from 6% in 1995 to 18% today, and recent ETF and mutual fund flows have reflected an incremental recent rotation from global equities to US equities.

Recent changes to index inclusion rules should accelerate the demand from passive funds for some of the potential impending IPO supply. FTSE Russell recently approved methodology changes to Russell US indices that would allow fast entry for large IPOs, following in the footsteps of changes to the Nasdaq-100 methodology earlier this month. The consultation on treatment of large IPOs held by S&P Dow Jones Indices closed for comments this past week.
